svg.text: Threat status buys a little monitoring. Record count buys all of it.
anyone planning to monitor threatened marine species from
whether this register can track a named species at all
the thin-record species are absent from the sea rather than
one row per bracket of total records — the rows are groups of species, not a sequence
share of the bracket's species with no record since 2016
Read down, not across: each row is a different group of species, sorted by
how many records they hold. The threatened dot is left of its control in
every row that matters, but the rows themselves span 72% to 1% — so how many
records a species already had decides this, and being listed shifts it a
little. 525 of 1,617 threatened species are in the top row.
and which groups it falls on
area is the number of threatened species in the class
share of the class's threatened species with no record since 2016
Seabirds lose 6% of their threatened species from the last decade and marine
mammals 10%; sea snails lose 67% and seagrasses 52%. Teleost fish contribute
the largest absolute number at 160. The dashed row is the fourteen species
IUCN lists as Extinct, at 85.7% — the control that shows the measure can
find an animal that is actually gone, median last sighting 1982.
OBIS v3 checklist/redlist and statistics/years, fetched 2026-09-18. IUCN does not assess from OBIS — assessments draw on literature, targeted survey
and expert judgement — so a Critically Endangered species with two records here is not an assessment resting on two observations; the question runs
the other way. OBIS stamps `category` only for CR, EN, VU and EX: Least Concern, Near Threatened and never-assessed all return null, so the controls
are drawn from same-family species with no category and matched on log10 records, not from 'unassessed' species, which this field cannot identify.
